newsitem.title: FINLAND: Yeltsin firm on NATO expansion at intense summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin firm on NATO expansion at intense summit.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin maintained his stiff opposition to NATO enlargement at summit talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday as the two men tackled the toughest issue dividing Moscow and the West.

Spokesmen for both sides described the initial two-hour session of talks as intense but not argumentative. Russian officials said there was progress on how to build better links between the 16-nation alliance and Moscow.

The talks on NATO and arms control were "substantive and intense", White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters. But no agreements had been reached so far and the two leaders would return to the subject in sessions later on Friday.

Asked if Yeltsin, who took a break before the afternoon sessions, had altered his position on NATO plans to take in former Soviet bloc states, Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said: "He did not change it even in nuance."

Meeting at the official residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari, a modern villa of granite and glass that overlooks the Baltic Sea, Clinton and Yeltsin adjourned after the morning talks to discuss Russia's economy over lunch.

Moscow bitterly opposes NATO's plans to take in former Soviet-bloc states in Eastern Europe, saying it would isolate and threaten Russia. Washington says NATO will take in new members as planned and that all Europe will benefit as a result.
A NATO summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start accession talks. The new members would not join until 1999 at the earliest.
"This was not an argument between these two presidents but really a very candid and thorough review of their different positions done in a very amicable spirit," McCurry said.
Clinton made the case for NATO enlargement "with a great deal of passion and conviction".

Yeltsin, under strong pressure from communist and nationalist critics at home who accuse him of selling out to the West, was apparently unmoved. He said earlier on Friday that he had not been convinced by Western arguments on NATO expansion.

But there was some progress, according to the Kremlin, on NATO's offer to forge a new, formal relationship with Russia that would give Moscow more of a say in European security without allowing it to veto alliance decisions.
Although Russia opposes NATO enlargement, it does want closer ties with its old Cold War foe and has been negotiating the terms of the relationship with the alliance.

"I have the impression that during these two hours the presidents not only advanced in understanding...but did more, in that they actually moved towards each other," Yastrzhembsky said, referring to NATO-Russia ties.

Yastrzhembsky said there could be a joint statement on European security when the talks end later on Friday. U.S. officials said there could be another four texts, covering nuclear arms cuts, missile defences, chemical weapons and economic issues.

Despite some thundering rhetoric from the Kremlin and displays of steely resolve from Washington in advance of the summit, the two leaders seemed upbeat before Friday's session, relying on their good personal relationship to see them through.

The two men are meeting for the 11th time, although they have not seen each other for almost a year. Clinton is confined to a wheelchair following a leg injury, while Yeltsin is still recovering from heart surgery and months of illness.
To make sure Yeltsin stands firm on NATO, his domestic opponents in the Russian parliament (Duma) planned a strident anti-Western debate on NATO for Friday.
Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov blasted Yeltsin's foreign policy before the debate, saying the president was incapable of defending Moscow's interests at the summit.
Clinton, too, is under pressure over NATO enlargement.

Eastern European nations, including the Baltic republics that lie just across the water from Helsinki, are watching closely to see there are no secret deals cut with Moscow over the future of Europe -- as in 1945, at the end of World War Two.
